title: The Loanable Funds Market
short: Saving supplies and borrowing demands loanable funds, and together they set the real interest rate.
trouble: Students mix up the money market (nominal rate, money supply and demand) with the loanable funds market (real rate, saving and borrowing), and shift the wrong curve when the government borrows.

blocks.html: The money market sets the nominal interest rate in the short run. A second market, built like any supply and demand market, shows how saving and borrowing set the Nominal and Real Interest Rates, and how government deficits fit in.

In the loanable funds market, the supply of loanable funds comes from saving (by households, by a government running a surplus, and by foreigners lending here) and the demand comes from borrowing (mainly firms investing, plus a government borrowing to cover a deficit). They set the real interest rate.

Savers lend more when the real return is higher, so supply slopes up. Borrowers invest in projects that pay more than the real interest rate, so at a lower rate more projects are worth doing: demand slopes down. Anything that changes saving at every rate shifts supply; anything that changes borrowing at every rate shifts demand. When the government borrows more, it competes with firms for the same pool of saving, so (in this course's framing) demand shifts right and the real rate rises.

blocks.cap: Try each event. Saving shifts supply; borrowing shifts demand. Notice the vertical axis: the real interest rate.

blocks.title: Which curve?
blocks.q: What happens to the real interest rate? (a) Households decide to save more. (b) An investment tax credit makes new factories more profitable.
steps: (a) More saving: supply shifts right, and the real rate falls.
(b) More borrowing for investment: demand shifts right, and the real rate rises.

blocks.title: Finding equilibrium
blocks.q: Supply: $r = 1 + 0.01Q$. Demand: $r = 9 - 0.01Q$ ($Q$ in billions, $r$ in percent). Find the equilibrium.

blocks.html: Mixing up the money market (nominal rate, money supply and demand) with the loanable funds market (real rate, saving and borrowing), and shifting the wrong curve when the government borrows. A deficit adds to the demand for loanable funds (some textbooks show it instead as less public saving, a leftward supply shift; the rate rises either way). Check: is the event about saving or about borrowing?
